semin-durr:129-129.t:
His saying: {تَخْلُدُونَ}: The majority read it in the light form (takhludūna), in the active voice. Qatāda read it with shadda (the intensive form), in the passive voice. To this belongs the saying of Imruʾ al-Qays:
3526 - وهَلْ يَنْعَمَنْ إلاَّ سَعِيْدٌ مُخَلَّدٌ ... قليلُ الهُمومِ ما يَبِيْتُ بأَوْجالِ
(Does anyone enjoy life but one who is fortunate and made to live forever, with few worries, who does not spend the night in fears?)
And «لَعَلَّ» (perhaps) here is in its ordinary sense. It is also said that it expresses cause (taʿlīl); this is supported by the reading of ʿAbd Allāh, «كي تَخْلُدون» ("so that you may live forever"). It is also said that it is for a question (istifhām); Zayd ibn ʿAlī said so, and so did the Kufans. It is also said that its meaning is comparison (tashbīh), i.e. "as though you will live forever"; this is supported by what is in the codex of Ubayy, «كأنكم تَخْلُدون». It was also read «كأنَّكم خالِدُون». And how many have stated explicitly that it can be for comparison.
And al-maṣāniʿ is the plural of maṣnaʿa, which is a water reservoir. It is also said: palaces. It is also said: dovecote towers.

semin-durr:130-130.t: His saying: {وَإِذَا بَطَشْتُمْ}: i.e. "and when you intend to seize". We needed to posit the implied "intention" only so that the protasis (sharṭ) and the apodosis (jazāʾ) would not be identical. And «جَبَّارِين» is a ḥāl (circumstantial).

semin-durr:132-132.t: His saying: {أَمَدَّكُمْ بِأَنْعَامٍ}: There are two possibilities. The first: the second clause is an explanation (bayān) of the first and an interpretation of it. The second: «بأَنْعامٍ» is a badal (substitute) for His saying {بِمَا تَعْلَمُونَ}, with repetition of the governing element, as in His saying {اتبعوا المرسلين اتبعوا مَن لاَّ يَسْأَلُكُمْ أَجْراً} [Yā Sīn: 20-21]. The Shaykh (Abū Ḥayyān) said: "Most scholars do not make this a badal; they make it a repetition (takrīr). They make something a badal with repetition of the governing element only when it is a preposition, without repeating what it is attached to (mutaʿalliq), such as: «I passed by Zayd, by your brother»; and they do not say «I passed by Zayd, I passed by your brother» as a badal."

semin-durr:136-136.t:
His saying: {أَمْ لَمْ تَكُنْ مِّنَ الواعظين}: It is the counterpart (muʿādil) of His saying {أَوَعَظْتَ}. The counterpart came in this form, rather than "أم لم تَعِظْ" ("or you do not admonish"), to keep the rhymes in agreement. Al-Zamakhsharī brought out a meaning for it and said: "There is a difference between them, for the meaning is: it is the same to us whether you have done this deed, which is admonition, or have never been one of its people or practitioners at all; this is stronger in expressing how little regard they have for his admonition, than saying «أم لم تَعِظْ»."
The majority read «أَوَعَظْتَ» with the ẓāʾ pronounced distinctly before the tāʾ. It is also reported from Abū ʿAmr, al-Kisāʾī and ʿĀṣim, and al-Aʿmash and Ibn Muḥayṣin read it, with assimilation (idghām). It is weak, because ẓāʾ is the stronger letter and the stronger is not assimilated into the weaker; although in the Noble Qurʾān there are several mutawātir (widely transmitted) cases of this sort which must be accepted, such as {زُحْزِحَ عَنِ} [Āl ʿImrān: 185] and {لَئِن بَسَطتَ} [al-Māʾida: 28].

semin-durr:137-137.t: His saying: {إِلاَّ خُلُقُ}: Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr and al-Kisāʾī read it with fatḥa on the khāʾ and sukūn on the lām (khalq). The others read it with two ḍammas (khuluq). It is said that the meaning of both is "fabrication" (ikhtilāq), which is lying; Ibn Masʿūd read it the same way. It is also said: what we are in, of constitution, life and death, is the character (khuluq) of the ancients and their custom. Al-Aṣmaʿī narrated from Nāfiʿ, and Abū Qilāba read it so, with ḍamma on the khāʾ and sukūn on the lām; it is a lightening of the form with two ḍammas.

semin-durr:147-147.t: His saying: {فِي جَنَّاتٍ}: It is a badal (substitute) for «فيما ههنا» ("in what is here"), with repetition of the governing element; it gives detail after a summary, as in the verse before it. And «ما» is a relative noun, and the adverb of place is its ṣila (relative clause).

semin-durr:148-148.t:
His saying: {وَنَخْلٍ}: It is possible that this belongs to the category of mentioning the specific after the general, because "gardens" (jannāt) include date palms. It is also possible that it is a repetition of one thing in another word, for they use "garden" (janna) and mean nothing but date palms. Zuhayr said:
3527 - كأنَّ عَيْنَيَّ في غَرْبَيْ مُقَتَّلةٍ ... من النَّواضِحِ تَسْقِي جَنَّةً سُحُقا
(As if my eyes were two buckets of a broken-in beast, one of the water-carrying camels, watering a garden of tall palms.)
/ And «سُحُقاً» is the plural of «سَحُوق», which is used to describe only date palms. And al-Ṭalʿ al-kufrā is the cluster of dates before it emerges from its sheath. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "The ṭalʿa is what comes out of the palm like the blade of a sword, in whose interior are the branches of the cluster (qinw). And the qinw is the name for what emerges from the trunk together with its stalk." And al-haḍīm is the delicate, from their saying «كَشْحٌ هضيمٌ» (a slender waist). It is also said: the densely packed.

semin-durr:149-149.t:
His saying: {وَتَنْحِتُونَ}: The majority read it in the second person with kasra on the ḥāʾ. Al-Ḥasan, ʿĪsā and Abū Ḥaywa read it with fatḥa on it. From al-Ḥasan also is «تَنْحاتون» with an alif for prolongation (ishbāʿ), and from him and from Abū Ḥaywa is «يَنْحِتُون» with yāʾ (third person). All of this has already been covered in al-Aʿrāf.
His saying: {فَارِهِينَ}: The Kufans and Ibn ʿĀmir read «فارِهيْنَ» with an alif, as they read «حاذِرون» with it; the others read «فَرِهين» without an alif, as they read «حَذِرُون» without it. Al-farāha is vigour and strength. It is also said: skill. One says «دابَّة فارِهٌ» (a sprightly mount) and does not say «فارِهَة»; and one says «فَرُه يَفْرُه فَراهة».

semin-durr:155-155.t: His saying: {لَّهَا شِرْبٌ}: It is a naʿt (adjective) of «ناقَةٌ». It is possible that the adjective is the preposition and its genitive noun alone, with «شِرْبٌ» as the fāʿil (agent) of it because it relies on (a preceding noun). Ibn Abī ʿAbla read «شُرْبٌ» with ḍamma in both places. Al-shirb with kasra is the share, like al-siqy (watering); with ḍamma it is the verbal noun.

semin-durr:168-168.t: His saying: {لِعَمَلِكُمْ}: It is like His saying {إِنِّي لَكُمَا لَمِنَ الناصحين} [al-Aʿrāf: 21], and that has already been covered. It is also said that «من القالِيْن» is a naʿt of an omitted khabar, and this preposition-phrase is attached to it, i.e. "I am one who hates your deed, of those who hate".

semin-durr:173-173.t:
His saying: {فَسَآءَ مَطَرُ المنذرين}: The one specified for blame (al-makhṣūṣ bi-l-dhamm) is omitted, i.e. "their rain". Al-qālī is the one who hates. One says «قَلاه يَقْليه قِلَىً» and «يَقْلاه», and the latter is irregular (shādhdha). He said:
3528 - وتَرْمِيْنَنِيْ بالطَّرْفِ أي: أنتَ مُذْنِبٌ ... وتَقْلِينني لكنَّ إياكِ لا أَقْلي
(You shoot me with a glance, meaning "you are guilty", and you hate me, but you I do not hate.)
And another said:
3529 - واللهِ ما فارَقْتُكم عَنْ قِلَىً لكمْ ... ولكنَّ ما يقضى فسوفَ يكونُ
(By Allah, I did not part from you out of hatred for you, but what is decreed will come to be.)
Its passive participle is «مَقْلِيّ». The original is «مَقْلُوْي»; then it was assimilated, like «مَرْمِيّ». He said:
3530 -. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... وَلسْتُ بمَقْلِيِّ الخِلالِ ولا قالِ
(... and I am not one whose qualities are hated, nor one who hates.)
i.e. no one else hates me and I hate no one. Some made a mistake and derived this from their saying «قلا اللحمَ» ("he roasted the meat"), as though it meant: he roasted his liver with hatred. The reason for the mistake is that this (the verb of hatred) belongs to the roots ending in yāʾ, while that belongs to the roots ending in wāw. One says «قلا اللحمَ يَقْلُوه قَلْواً», so he is «قالٍ» like «غازٍ», and the object is «مَقْلُوٌّ».

semin-durr:184-184.t:
His saying: {الجبلة}: The majority read it with kasra on the jīm and the bāʾ and shadda on the lām. Abū Ḥuṣayn, al-Aʿmash and al-Ḥasan read it with ḍamma on both and shadda on the lām. Al-Sulamī read it with fatḥa on the jīm, or kasra, with sukūn on the bāʾ. These are dialectal variants of this word, and its meaning is: the united, thick creation, taken from al-jabal (the mountain). The poet said:
3532 - والمَوْتُ أعظمُ حادِثٍ ... فيما يَمُرُّ على الجِبِلَّهْ
(Death is the greatest event among what passes over creation.)
Al-Mahdawī said: "Al-jibl, al-jabl and al-jubl are dialectal variants, and it is the large multitude of people. It is also said: al-jibilla is from their saying «جُبِل على كذا», i.e. he was created and disposed upon it. The full discussion of that will come in Yā Sīn, God willing, at His saying {جِبِلاًّ كَثِيراً} [Yā Sīn: 62], together with the differences of the readers on it."
[Translator's note: the opening quotation mark of al-Mahdawī's statement is not closed in the source.]

semin-durr:186-186.t: His saying: {وَمَآ أَنتَ}: In the story of Hūd it came as «ما أنت» without wāw, and here as «وما أنت» with wāw. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "When the wāw enters, two meanings are intended, each of them contrary to messengership in their view: being bewitched/subjected (taskhīr) and being human, and that a messenger may be neither bewitched nor human. When the wāw is omitted, only one meaning is intended, which is his being bewitched, and then he confirmed it with his being human." The disagreement over «كِسَفاً» and its derivation was covered in al-Isrāʾ.

semin-durr:192-192.t: His saying: {وَإِنَّهُ لَتَنزِيلُ}: The pronoun hāʾ refers to the Qurʾān, even though it has not been mentioned, because of its being known. And «تنزيل» has the meaning of «مُنَزَّل» (sent down), or there is an omitted muḍāf, i.e. "the one who has a revelation (dhū tanzīl)".

semin-durr:193-193.t: His saying: {نَزَلَ}: Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr and Ḥafṣ read «نَزَل» in the light form. And {الروح الأمين} are both nominative, with the verb attributed to al-Rūḥ, and al-Amīn is its naʿt; what is meant by it is Jibrīl. The rest of the Seven read it with shadda in the active voice, the agent being Allah the Exalted: «الروحَ الأمينَ» are both accusative as the object. And «الروحُ الأمينُ» (is also read) both nominative, on the basis of the passive (what has no named agent). And «به» is either attached to «نَزَلَ» or to an omitted element, as a ḥāl.

semin-durr:194-194.t: His saying: {على قَلْبِكَ لِتَكُونَ}: The Shaykh (Abū Ḥayyān) said: The apparent sense is that «على قلبِك» and «لتكون» are attached to «نَزَل», and he did not mention what stands against this apparent sense. The most that can be imagined is that they may be attached to «تنزيل», i.e. "and it is the revelation of the Lord of the Worlds upon your heart, that you may be". But there is weakness in it, in that the maṣdar is separated from its object by the clause «نَزَلَ به الروحُ». This can be answered in two ways. The first: that this clause is parenthetical (iʿtirāḍiyya) and contains emphasis and rectification, so it is not foreign. The second: tolerance is allowed in the adverbial and its like. On this basis it is not far-fetched for the rule of iʿmāl (competing governance) to apply in the matter, for each of «تنزيل» and «نَزَل» demands these two prepositional phrases.

semin-durr:195-195.t: His saying: {بِلِسَانٍ}: It may be attached to «المُنْذِرين», i.e. "that he may be among those who warned in this Arabic tongue", namely Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, Shuʿayb, Ismāʿīl and Muḥammad ﷺ. It may also be attached to «نَزَلَ», i.e. "it was sent down in the Arabic tongue so that you may warn by it", because had it been sent down in a non-Arabic tongue, they would have said: "Why has been sent down to us what we do not understand?" Abū l-Baqāʾ allowed that it be a badal from «به» with repetition of the governing element. He said: "i.e. it was sent down in an Arabic tongue, i.e. in a message or a language."

semin-durr:196-196.t: His saying: {وَإِنَّهُ لَفِي زُبُرِ}: i.e. "and indeed the Qurʾān". It is also said: "and indeed Muḥammad". There is an iltifāt (shift of person) in it, since had it followed what preceded it would have said: "and indeed you are in the scriptures". Al-Aʿmash read «زُبْرِ» with sukūn on the bāʾ, a lightened form of the well-known one.

semin-durr:176-176.t:
His saying: {الأيكة}: Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr and Ibn ʿĀmir read «لَيْكَةَ» with a single lām and fatḥa on the tāʾ. They made it a noun not made definite by al-, with «أصحاب» annexed to it, here and in Ṣād specifically. The others read «الأَيْكَةِ», made definite by al-, in agreement with what is agreed upon in al-Ḥijr and in Qāf.
The statements of people about the first reading have been in disarray, and some of them were bold against its reciter. I shall mention part of that for you. Its justification, according to what Abū ʿUbayd said, is: "that «لَيْكَة» is the name of the village they were in, and «الأيْكَة» is the name of the whole land. Abū ʿUbayd said: "I do not like departing from the written form in anything of the Qurʾān, except for what goes outside the speech of the Arabs; and this does not go outside their speech, with the soundness of the meaning in these words. That is because we found in some exegesis a distinction between laykah and al-aykah. It was said: laykah is the name of the village they were in, and al-aykah is the whole land, so the difference between them became like that between Bakka and Makka. I also saw them, in what is said to be the Imām, the codex of ʿUthmān, as separate: I found the ones in al-Ḥijr and Qāf to be «الأَيْكَة», and I found the ones in al-Shuʿarāʾ and Ṣād to be «لَيْكَة». Then the codices of the regions agreed upon them afterwards, and we do not know that they differed on them. The people of Madina read according to this wording that we have related, meaning without alif and lām and without the declension (i.e. as a diptote)." End of what Abū ʿUbayd said. The Shaykh Shihāb al-Dīn Abū Shāma said after I quoted it from him: "This is his wording and it is not sound, for the lām is present in «لَيْكة»; the correct form is 'without alif and hamza'." I say: Rather it is sound, for he means without the alif and lām of definiteness, not without any lām at all.
Abū ʿUbayd's statement has been followed up and they objected to him. Abū Jaʿfar said: "The readers agreed on the genitive for the one in al-Ḥijr and Qāf, so what is disputed / should be returned to what is agreed upon, when the meaning is one. As for what Abū ʿUbayd related, that «ليكَةَ» is the name of the village and al-Aykah is the name of the whole land, it is a thing not established, and it is not known who said it; and were he known, there would be consideration in it, because the people of knowledge altogether, among the exegetes and those who know the speech of the Arabs, are against it. We know of no disagreement among the people of the language that al-aykah is the entangled trees. As for the argument of some who argued for the reading of those who read in these two places with fatḥa, that in the written text (al-sawād) it is «لَيْكة», there is no proof in it. The statement on it is that its original is «الأَيْكَة»; then the hamza was lightened and its vowel was cast onto the lām, and it (the hamza) dropped, and you did without the alif of connection since the lām was now vowelled. On this basis only the genitive is permissible, as you say «مررتُ بالأَحْمَرِ» with the hamza pronounced fully, then you lighten it and say «بِلَحْمَرِ». If you wish you write it in the script as you wrote it first, and if you wish you write it with the omission, and only the genitive is allowed. Therefore in «الأَيْكَةِ» only the genitive is allowed."
Sībawayh said: "Know that everything that is not declined (diptote), when alif and lām enter it or you annex it, becomes declined." We know of no one who contradicted Sībawayh in this.
And al-Mubarrad said in the Book of Orthography (Kitāb al-Khaṭṭ): "In some places they wrote «كَذَّبَ أصحابُ لَيْكَة» without alif, because the alif drops in connected speech. For that reason the reader who read it with fatḥa made a mistake, imagining that «لَيْكَةَ» is the name of something and that the lām is a root letter, so he read: aṣḥābu laykata." Al-Farrāʾ said: "We consider, and Allah knows best, that it was written in these two places with the hamza omitted, so the alif dropped because of the vowelling of the lām." Makkī said: Ibn Qutayba followed up on Abū ʿUbayd and chose «الأَيْكَةِ» with alif, hamza and genitive. He said: "It was only written without alif on the basis of lightening the hamza." He said: "People have agreed on that, meaning in al-Ḥijr and Qāf, so what is in al-Shuʿarāʾ and Ṣād must be joined to what they agreed upon, for what they agreed upon is a witness for what they differed on."
And Abū Isḥāq (al-Zajjāj) said: "The reading with the genitive of His saying «ليكةِ», meaning «الأيكة», is better than making it «لَيْكَةَ» and putting fatḥa on it, because it would be a diptote; but «لَيْكَة» is not made definite, and it is only «أَيْكة» for the singular and «أَيْك» for the plural, like «أَجَمَة» and «أَجَم». And al-ayk is the entangled trees. So the best reading of it is the kasra with the omission of the hamza, in agreement with the codex, and I know of it only that it has been read thus."
And al-Fārisī said: "The statement of one who said «ليكةَ», putting fatḥa on the tāʾ, is problematic, because he put fatḥa while the lām is attached to the word. This is, in its impossibility, like the saying of one who says «مَرَرْتُ بِلَحْمَرَ», putting fatḥa on the end while the lām of definiteness is attached. It was only written «لَيْكَةَ» on the basis of lightening the hamza, and fatḥa is not sound in Arabic, because it is putting fatḥa on the case-ending letter in a genitive position along with the lām of definiteness, so it follows the analogy of the saying of one who says «مررتُ بلَحْمَرَ». And it is remote that Nāfiʿ would put fatḥa on that, given what Warsh said from him."
I say: He means that Warsh transmitted from Nāfiʿ the transfer of the vowel of the hamza to the preceding quiescent letter, wherever it occurs, with stated conditions; and among that is what is in sūrat al-Ḥijr and Qāf, the word «الأيكة». So he read, in accordance with his principle, in the two sūras, by transferring the vowel, dropping the hamza and putting kasra on the yāʾ-bearing letter; so the ruling should be the same in these two places too.
And al-Zamakhsharī said: "«أصحابُ الأَيْكة» has been read with the hamza, with its lightening, and with the genitive by annexation, and that is the right way. As for the one who read it with the accusative and claimed that laykah, on the pattern of laylah, is the name of a land, it is a misconception to which the script of the codex led him. It was written only in accordance with the pronunciation of the speaker, as the grammarians write [it], because … in this form to show the lightened pronunciation. It was written in the rest of the Qurʾān in its original form, and the story is one. Moreover «لَيْكَة» is a name that is not known." It is related that the people of al-Aykah were people of entangled trees and their tree was the dūm (doum palm). That is, the root l-y-k is absent from the tongue of the Arabs; so said the investigators of those who traced that. He said: "This is as they stated that the two dotted letters khāʾ and dhāl never combine with jīm in the language of the Arabs." For that reason the author of al-Ṣiḥāḥ did not mention it, despite his mentioning the distinction reported earlier from Abū ʿUbayd; had it existed in the language he would have mentioned it along with mentioning the distinction reported earlier, given the great need for it.
[Translator's note: the sentence beginning "because … in this form" has a gap in the source text, marked by ". . ." in the Arabic.]
And al-Zajjāj also said: "The people of Madina put fatḥa, according to what came in the exegesis, that the name of the city in which Shuʿayb was is Laykah." Abū ʿAlī said: "If this were sound, then why / did the readers agree on the hamza in His saying {وَإِن كَانَ أَصْحَابُ الأيكة} [verse 78] in al-Ḥijr? The Aykah mentioned here is the Aykah mentioned there. And Ibn ʿAbbās said: «الأَيْكَةُ: الغَيْضَةُ» (al-Aykah is the thicket), and he did not interpret it as the city or the land."
I say: All of these people, it is as if they claimed that these established imāms took this reading only from the script of the codices rather than from the mouths of men. How can such be thought of the eldest of the readers and the highest of them in chain of transmission, who took the Qurʾān from a number of the great Companions, Abū l-Dardāʾ, ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān and others, and of the likes of the imām of Mecca, may Allah the Exalted honour it, and the likes of the imām of Madina? And how can Abū ʿUbayd's statement be denied, or he be accused in his transmission? One who has memorized is a proof against one who has not memorized, and tawātur (mass transmission) is definitive, so it is not opposed by what is conjectural.
As for the difference of reading with the unity of the story, that does no harm: it was expressed sometimes by "the village" specifically, and sometimes by "the city" that gathers all the villages and includes them. As for Ibn ʿAbbās' interpretation, it does not contradict that, because he expressed it by what is abundant in it. Whoever sees what I mentioned of the merits of these imāms in my commentary on Ḥirz al-Amānī will set aside what they were attacked with, and will know their worth and standing. And Abū l-Baqāʾ said about this reading: "This is not correct, since there is no «لَيْكة» in the speech such that it could be made a proper name. And if it is claimed that the hamza was turned into a lām, that is extremely remote." I say:
3531 - وابنُ اللَّبونِ إذا ما لُزَّ في قَرَنٍ ... لم يَسْتَطِعْ صَوْلَةَ البُزْلِ القَناعيسِ
(The young camel in its third year, when it is yoked in a rope, cannot withstand the onslaught of the strong, sturdy adult camels.)
«أطرقْ كرا إنَّ النِّعامِ بالقرى» ("Be silent, kara [a bird]; the ostriches are in the villages")
«مَنْ أنت وزيداً» ("Who are you and Zayd?")
[Translator's note: the source ends with the verse and the two sayings without any connecting comment, apparently as examples of irregular or fragmentary usage; the link to the preceding discussion is not stated in the text.]

semin-durr:197-197.t:
His saying: {أَوَ لَمْ يَكُن لَّهُمْ آيَةً}: Ibn ʿĀmir read «تكن» with tāʾ (feminine) and «آيةٌ» in the nominative. The others read «يكنْ» with yāʾ (masculine) and «آيةً» in the accusative. Ibn ʿAbbās read «تكن» with tāʾ and «آيةً» in the accusative. As for Ibn ʿĀmir's reading, «تكون» may be complete (tāmma) or defective (nāqiṣa). If it is complete, it is possible that «لهم» is attached to it and «آيةٌ» is its fāʿil (agent). And «أَنْ يعلَمَه» is either a badal from «آية» or the khabar of an implied mubtadaʾ, i.e. "Has there not occurred for them a sign, the knowledge of the scholars of the Children of Israel?"
If it is defective, four possibilities are allowed. The first: that its ism is a latent pronoun in it meaning "the matter" (qiṣṣa), and «آيةٌ أَنْ يَعْلَمَه» is a clause in which the khabar is placed first, standing in the position of the khabar of «تكن». The second: that its ism is also the pronoun of the matter, with «لهم» a fronted khabar and «آيةٌ» a postponed mubtadaʾ, the clause being the khabar of «تكن»; and «أَنْ يعلَمَه» is either a badal from «آيةٌ» or the khabar of an implied mubtadaʾ, i.e. "it is that they know it." The third: that «لهم» is the khabar of «تكنْ» fronted before its ism, and «آيةٌ» is its ism, and «أَنْ يعلَمَه» takes the two previous possibilities: being a badal, or the khabar of an implied mubtadaʾ. The fourth: that «آيةٌ» is its ism and «أَنْ يعلمَه» is its khabar. This has been objected to, in that it requires making the ism indefinite and the khabar definite. Some have stated that this is a necessity (of poetry), as in his saying:
3533 -. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... ولا يَكُ مَوْقِفٌ منكِ الوَداعا
(... and let not a standing-place from you be the farewell.)
and his saying:
3534 -. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... يكون مزاجَها عَسَلٌ وماءُ
(... its mixture is honey and water.)
An excuse has been made for that: that «آية» has been specified by His saying «لهم», for it is a ḥāl from it, and the ḥāl is a description; and that definiteness by genus is weak because of its generality. This is a false excuse, and no necessity calls for this analysis; rather the analysis is what has preceded.
As for the reading of the others, it is very clear: «آيةً» is a fronted khabar, «أَنْ يَعْلَمه» is its postponed ism, and «لهم» is attached to «آية», or is a ḥāl from «آية».
As for Ibn ʿAbbās' reading, it is like the reading {ثُمَّ لَمْ تَكُنْ فِتْنَتَهم إلاَّ أَنْ قَالوا} [al-Anʿām: 23] and like the saying of Labīd:
3535 - فمضَى وقدَّمها وكانت عادَةً ... منه إذا هي عَرَّدَتْ إقدامُها
(He went on and sent it forward, and it was his custom, when it shied away, to press it forward.)
either because of the femininity of the ism for the femininity of the khabar, or because it has the meaning of a feminine. Do you not see that «أَنْ يعلَمَه» is equivalent to "the knowledge", and «إلاَّ أَنْ قالوا» equivalent to "their saying", and «إقدامها» to "its pressing forward"?
Al-Jaḥdarī read «أَنْ تعلمَه» with tāʾ. He likened "sons" (banīn) to the broken plural in the change of its singular's form, so he treated its verb, when predicated of it, as he treats its verb in taking the sign of the feminine. This is like his saying:
3536 - قالَتْ بنو عامرٍ خالُوا بني أَسَدٍ ... يا بؤسَ للجَهْلِ ضَرَّاراً لأَقْوامِ
(The Banū ʿĀmir said: "Leave the Banū Asad alone." Alas for ignorance, how harmful it is to peoples!)
In the noble orthography they wrote «عُلَمؤا» with a wāw after the mīm, followed by the alif. It is said: this is according to the dialect of those who incline the alif toward wāw, as was done in ṣalāh and zakāh.

semin-durr:198-198.t:
His saying: {الأعجمين}: The author of al-Taḥrīr said: "Al-aʿjamīn is the plural of aʿjamī with lightening. Were it not for this assumption, it could not be pluralised as a sound plural." I say: the reason for preventing its pluralisation is that it belongs to the pattern afʿal, feminine faʿlāʾ, like aḥmar, ḥamrāʾ.
The Basrans allow its sound plural only by poetic necessity, as in his saying:
3537 -. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... حلائلَ أَسْوَدِيْنَ وأَحْمَرينا
(... wives of black men and red men.)
So he assumed it to be a relative adjective (mansūb) and lightened the yāʾ. Ibn ʿAṭiyya made it the plural of aʿjam. He said: "Al-aʿjamūn is the plural of aʿjam / which is the one who is not fluent; even if Arab by lineage, he is called aʿjam, and this is said of animals. To this belongs his saying ﷺ: «جُرْحُ العجماء جُبار» (the wound inflicted by a dumb beast is not compensated)." Al-Ṭabarī reported with chain from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muṭīʿ that he was standing at ʿArafa with a camel beneath him and said: "This camel of mine is aʿjam; and if it were sent down upon it, they would not believe." "And al-ʿajamī is the one whose attribution is to the non-Arabs (al-ʿajam), even if he is the most fluent of people."
Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Al-aʿjam is the one who is not fluent, and in whose tongue there is ʿujma or istiʿjām (inarticulacy). Al-aʿjamī is the same, except that it has the addition of the attributive (nisba) for emphasis." I say: something like this has already been covered in Sūrat al-Naḥl. Abū l-Baqāʾ explicitly forbade that «الأعجمين» be the plural of «أَعْجم», saying it is only the plural of aʿjamī, lightened from aʿjamī, like «الأَشْعرون» for al-Ashʿarī. He said: "«الأعجمين» [i.e.] «الأعجميين», so he dropped the yāʾ of attribution as they said «الأشعرون», i.e. «الأشعريُّون», and its singular is aʿjamī. It cannot be the plural of aʿjam because its feminine is ʿajmāʾ, and the like of this is not pluralised as a sound plural."
I say: that has already been covered. In what Ibn ʿAṭiyya said there is something to consider. As for al-Zamakhsharī, there is nothing in his statement that it is the plural of aʿjam lightened or not lightened, although his apparent meaning is that it is the plural of aʿjam without lightening. But what Ibn ʿAṭiyya said, he followed al-Farrāʾ in it, for he said: "«الأعجمين» is the plural of aʿjam or of aʿjamī, with the yāʾ of attribution dropped, as they said «الأشعرين», whose singular is Ashʿarī." And he recited from al-Kumayt:
3538 - ولو جَهَّزْتَ قافيةً شَرُوْدا ... لقد دَخَلَتْ بيوتَ الأَشْعَريْنا
(Even if you had sent forth a far-travelling verse, it would have entered the houses of the Ashʿarīs.)
But this does not harm al-Farrāʾ, for he is among the Kufans, and I have already mentioned that they allow the pluralisation of afʿal faʿlāʾ.
Al-Ḥasan and Ibn Miqsam read «الأَعْجميِّين» with two yāʾs of attribution, which supports the lightening of it from this in the reading of the majority.

semin-durr:200-200.t: His saying: {كَذَلِكَ سَلَكْنَاهُ}: i.e. "like that", or "the matter is thus". The pronoun in «سَلَكْناه» refers to the Qurʾān, and this is the apparent sense, i.e. "We made it enter the hearts of the criminals as We made it enter the hearts of the believers", and despite that it did not take effect in them. It is also said: it refers to denial or to disbelief.

semin-durr:201-201.t: His saying: {لاَ يُؤْمِنُونَ بِهِ}: There are two possibilities for this clause. The first: it is resumptive (istiʾnāf), by way of explanation and clarification of what precedes it. The second: it is a ḥāl from the pronoun in «سَلَكْناه», i.e. "We made it enter, not being believed in". It is also possible that it is a ḥāl from «المجرمين», because the muḍāf is a part of the muḍāf ilayhi.

semin-durr:202-202.t:
His saying: {فَيَأْتِيَهُم}: And «فيقولوا» is conjoined to «يَرَوْا». The majority read it with yāʾ (masculine). Al-Ḥasan and ʿĪsā read it with tāʾ (feminine). They made the pronoun of the punishment feminine because it has the meaning of "chastisement" (ʿuqūba). Al-Zamakhsharī said: "It was made feminine on the basis that the agent is the pronoun of the Hour." And al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you ask: what is the meaning of sequence (taʿqīb) in His saying «فَيَأْتِيَهم»? I say: the meaning is not sequence in existence, but rather the ordering of them in severity. It is as if it were said: they will not believe in the Qurʾān until their seeing the punishment, [and what is] more severe than it. An example of that is that you say: 'If you do wrong, the righteous will loathe you, and then Allah will loathe you', for by this ordering you do not intend that Allah's loathing comes after the loathing of the righteous; your intention is only the ordering of the severity of the matter upon the wrongdoer."
And al-Ḥasan read «بَغَتَةً» with fatḥa on the ghayn.

semin-durr:205-205.t: His saying: {أَفَرَأَيْتَ}: Its detailed treatment has already been covered. «أفرأيت» and «جاءهم» compete (tanāzaʿa) over His saying «ما كانوا يُمَتَّعون». If you give effect to the second, which is «جاءهم», you make «ما كانوا» nominative by it as its agent; and the first object of «أرأَيْتَ» is its pronoun, but it is omitted, and the second object is the interrogative clause in His saying «ما أَغْنَى عنهم». There must be a link between this clause and the omitted first object, and it is implied, its implied form being: "Have you considered what they were being promised, how did their enjoyment avail them when it came, i.e. what was promised?" The force of the speech indicates that. If you give effect to the first, you make «ما كانوا يُوْعَدُون» accusative by it and you place in «جاءهم» its pronoun as agent; and the interrogative clause is also the second object. The returning pronoun is implied as established in the previous analysis, and the conditional is parenthetical, its apodosis omitted. All of this is understood from what preceded in Sūrat al-Anʿām. I mentioned it here only because it is a difficult assumption that requires reflection and good craftsmanship. All of this works out only on our view that «ما» is interrogative, and their interpreting it as negation does not harm us, since an interrogative may come with the meaning of negation. But if you make it a negative particle, as Abū l-Baqāʾ said, that does not work, because the second object of «أرأيت» can only be an interrogative clause, as has been established more than once.

semin-durr:207-207.t:
His saying: {مَآ أغنى}: «ما» may be interrogative, in the accusative position as a fronted object, with «ما كانوا» as the fāʿil, and the «ما» (in the latter) a maṣdar particle, meaning: "What did their being enjoyers avail them?" Or it may be negative, with the object omitted, i.e. "Their enjoyment did not avail them anything."
It was also read «يُمْتَعُون» with sukūn on the mīm and lightening of the tāʾ, from «أَمْتَع اللهُ زيداً بكذا».

semin-durr:208-208.t:
His saying: {إِلاَّ لَهَا مُنذِرُونَ}: The clause may be a naʿt (adjective) of «قريةٍ», or a ḥāl from it. What allows that is the preceding negation. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you ask: how did you remove the wāw from the clause after «إلاَّ», while it was not removed in His saying {وَمَآ أَهْلَكْنَا مِن قَرْيَةٍ إِلاَّ وَلَهَا كِتَابٌ مَّعْلُومٌ} [al-Ḥijr: 4]? I say: the rule is to remove the wāw, because the clause is an adjective of «قريةٍ». When it is added, it is to emphasize the connection of the adjective to the described, as in His saying {سَبْعَةٌ وَثَامِنُهُمْ كَلْبُهُمْ} [al-Kahf: 22]." The Shaykh (Abū Ḥayyān) said: "Had we assumed «لها مُنْذِرُون» to be a clause, it could not come as an adjective after «إلاَّ»."
The position of the majority is that an adjective does not come after «إلاَّ» when relying on the particle of exception, as in «ما جاءَني أحدٌ إلاَّ راكبٌ» ("No one came to me except a rider"). When something like this is heard, they analyse it as a badal, i.e. "except a man, a rider". What proves the soundness of this position is that the Arabs say «ما مررتُ بأحدٍ إلاَّ قائماً» ("I did not pass by anyone except standing") and «إلاَّ قائمٍ» in the genitive is not preserved from them. Were the clause an adjective after «إلاَّ», the genitive would be heard in this. [Also, if the clause were an adjective of an indefinite noun, it would be possible for an adjective of a definite noun to occur after «إلاَّ», meaning like: «ما مررتُ بزيدٍ إلاَّ العاقلِ».]
Then he said: "If the adjective does not rely on the particle, the adjective may come after «إلاَّ», as in «ما جاءني أحدٌ إلاَّ زيدٌ خيرٌ من عمروٍ». The implied form: «ما جاءني أحدٌ خيرٌ من عمرٍو إلاَّ زيدٌ». As for the wāw being added to emphasize the connection of the adjective with the described, it is not familiar in the wording of the grammarians. If you said «جاءني رجلٌ وعاقلٌ», meaning «رجلٌ عاقلٌ», it would not be permissible. The wāw enters adjectives, permissibly, only when some are conjoined to others and their significations differ, as in «مررت بزيدٍ الشجاعِ والشاعرِ». As for {وَثَامِنُهُمْ كَلْبُهُمْ} [al-Kahf: 22], the discussion of it has already been covered."
I say: As for the adjective not occurring after «إلاَّ» when relying on it, al-Zamakhsharī chooses otherwise, for it is a disputed question. As for the fact that «إلاَّ قائماً» in the accusative is said and not «قائم» in the genitive, that is one of two permissible options, and there is no proof in it for forbidding its counterpart. As for his saying "it is not familiar from the speech of the grammarians", that is not conceded: this is Ibn Jinnī, who stated it in some of his books. As for his imposing the consequence that, if the clause were an adjective of an indefinite after «إلاَّ», an adjective of a definite could occur after «إلاَّ», it is not necessary, because that is specific to the adjective being a clause; and when it is a clause, its being an adjective of a definite is impossible. That is specific to the adjective being a clause because (the wāw) is for emphasizing the connection of the adjective, and emphasis befits the clause. As for his saying "if you said «جاءني رجلٌ وعاقلٌ» it would not be permissible", it is conceded, but that is prevented only in a non-clause, for in a clause confusion is absent. {سَبْعَةٌ وَثَامِنُهُمْ} has already been covered, so let it be consulted there.

semin-durr:209-209.t:
His saying: {ذكرى}: Several possibilities are allowed for it. The first: it is a mafʿūl li-ajlihi (object of purpose). If it is an object of purpose, there are two views on its governor. The first: «مُنْذِرُوْن», the meaning being "warners for the sake of admonition and reminder". The second: «أَهْلَكْنا». Al-Zamakhsharī said: "The meaning is: We did not destroy any wrongdoing people of a township except after We had imposed the proof upon them by sending warners to them, so that [their destruction] would be a reminder and lesson for others, that they not disobey as these disobeyed." Then he said: "This is the view relied upon."
The Shaykh (Abū Ḥayyān) said: "There is nothing to rely upon in this, for the position of the majority is that what is before «إلاَّ» does not govern what is after it, unless it is the excepted, or the one from which exception is made, or a follower of it not relying on the particle, as in «ما مررت بأحدٍ إلاَّ زيدٌ من عمروٍ»; and the object of purpose is none of these. His position can be analysed on the position of al-Kisāʾī and al-Akhfash, although they did not state the object of purpose specifically." I say: the answer is what preceded earlier, that he chooses the position of al-Akhfash.
The second of the first possibilities: it is in the nominative position as the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, i.e. "this is a reminder"; and the clause is parenthetical. The third: it is a naʿt of «مُنْذِرُوْن»: either by way of exaggeration, or by omission, i.e. "warners possessing a reminder", or by the maṣdar taking the place of the active participle, i.e. "warners, reminders". The explanation of that has already been covered. The fourth: it is in the accusative position as a ḥāl, i.e. "reminding", or "possessing a reminder", or they were made the very reminder, for exaggeration. The fifth: it is accusative as an emphasizing maṣdar (maṣdar muʾakkid).
Then there are two views on its governor: the first, the word «مُنْذِرُون», because it is from its meaning, so the two are like «قَعَدْتُ جلوساً». The second: that it is omitted, from its own word, i.e. "you are reminded with a reminder"; and that omitted verb is an adjective of «مُنْذِرون».

semin-durr:210-210.t:
His saying: {وَمَا تَنَزَّلَتْ بِهِ الشياطين}: The majority read it with yāʾ / and a ḍamma on the nūn, and it is a broken plural. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Ibn al-Samayfaʿ and al-Aʿmash read it with wāw in place of yāʾ, and the nūn with fatḥa, treating it as a sound plural. This reading was rejected by a great many grammarians. Al-Farrāʾ said: "The Shaykh made a mistake; he thought it was the nūn that comes on two letters (i.e. a root letter)." Al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl said: "If it is allowed to argue from the saying of al-ʿAjjāj and Ruʾba, why is it not allowed to argue from the saying of al-Ḥasan and his companion, meaning Muḥammad ibn al-Samayfaʿ? And we know that they read it thus only because they had heard it." Al-Naḥḥās said: "It is a mistake according to all the grammarians." Al-Mahdawī said: "It is not permissible in Arabic." Abū Ḥātim said: "It is a mistake from him or against him."
A group of the people of knowledge affirmed this reading and repelled the mistake from it, for the reciter of it was in a firm position of knowledge, and they answered it with sound answers. Al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl said: "Yūnus ibn Ḥabīb said: I heard a Bedouin say: «دَخلتُ بساتينَ من ورائِها بساتُون» ('I entered orchards, behind which are bastūn'), and I said: how similar this is to the reading of al-Ḥasan." Some analysed it as the plural of «شَيَّاط» with shadda, an intensive pattern like «ضَرَّاب» and «قتَّال», being derived from «شاط يَشِيْط», i.e. he burned; then it was pluralised as a sound plural with lightening of the yāʾ, so its pattern is faʿālūn, lightened from faʿʿālīn with shadda on the ʿayn. What indicates that is that the two (readers) and others read it so, I mean with shadda on the yāʾ. This is transmitted from Muʾarrij al-Sadūsī. Others justified it thus: since its ending resembles the ending of «يَبْرِين» and «فِلَسْطين», its inflection was applied sometimes on the nūn, and sometimes on the letter (wāw/yāʾ), as they said: «هذه يَبْرِينُ وفِلَسْطينُ» and «يبرونَ وفلسطونَ». The discussion of this has already been covered in al-Baqara.
And the hāʾ in «به» refers to the Qurʾān.
These three clauses came negated in the best order: first he negated the Satans' bringing it down, because negation is mostly of the possible, even though possibility here is itself negated. Then he secondly negated the appropriateness of that, i.e. even if possibility were supposed, they would not be fit for it. Then he thirdly negated ability and power, then mentioned the reason for that, which is their being cut off from listening to the Highest Assembly, for they are pelted with shooting stars if they try to listen.

semin-durr:213-213.t: His saying: {فَتَكُونَ}: It is accusative in response to a prohibition (jawāb al-nahy).

semin-durr:216-216.t: His saying: {فَإِنْ عَصَوْكَ}: There are two views on this wāw. The first: it is the pronoun of the disbelievers, i.e. "if the disbelievers disobey you in your command to them to affirm Oneness". The second: it is the pronoun of the believers, i.e. "if the believers disobey you in the branches of Islam and some of the rulings after they have believed you and believed in your message". This is extremely remote.

semin-durr:217-217.t: His saying: {وَتَوكَّلْ}: Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir read it with fāʾ. The others read it with wāw. As for the reading with fāʾ, he made what comes after the fāʾ like a consequence (jazāʾ) of what precedes it, following from it; and the reading with wāw is merely for conjoining one clause to another.

semin-durr:218-218.t: His saying: {الذي يَرَاكَ}: It may be in the nominative position as the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, or accusative for praise (madḥ), or genitive as a naʿt, badal or bayān.

semin-durr:219-219.t: His saying: {وَتَقَلُّبَكَ}: It is conjoined to the object of «يَراك», i.e. "and He sees your moving about". This is the reading of the majority. Janāḥ ibn Ḥubaysh read it with yāʾ (with ḍamma), kasra on the lām and ḍamma on the bāʾ, making it a verb, the imperfect of «قَلَّب» with shadda, and conjoined it to the imperfect before it, which is «يراك», i.e. "He who turns you about".

semin-durr:221-221.t: His saying: {على مَن تَنَزَّلُ}: It is attached to «تَنَزَّلُ» which follows it. It was fronted only because it has the right to the beginning of the speech (interrogatives), and it suspends (muʿalliq) the verb of informing before it, because that verb has the meaning of knowing. It is possible that here it takes two objects, so that the clause containing the interrogative stands in the place of the second, since the first is the pronoun of the addressees; and it is possible that it takes three, so that it stands in the place of two. Al-Bazzī read «على مَنْ تَّنَزَّلُ» with shadda on the tāʾ [of tanazzal] in both places; the original is «تَتَنَزَّلُ» with two tāʾs, which was assimilated. Assimilation in the second is easy because what precedes the assimilated letter is vowelled; in the first there is difficulty because what precedes it is quiescent, namely the nūn of «مَنْ». The detailed treatment of this has already been covered in al-Baqara at His saying {وَلاَ تَيَمَّمُواْ الخبيث} [al-Baqara: 267].

semin-durr:223-223.t:
His saying: {يُلْقُونَ}: The pronoun may refer to «الشياطين», in which case the clause «يُلْقُون» may be a ḥāl, or resumptive. The meaning of their "casting the hearing" is: their listening attentively to the Highest Assembly in order to steal something; or they cast the thing heard to the soothsayers. It is also possible that it refers to {كُلِّ أَفَّاكٍ أَثِيمٍ} insofar as it is plural in meaning. Then the clause is either resumptive or a naʿt of «كلِّ أَفَّاكٍ», and the meaning of the casting is as stated before.
The Shaykh (Abū Ḥayyān), in the case where the pronoun refers to «الشياطين», after mentioning the two previous meanings of casting the hearing, said: "On the meaning of listening attentively, «يُلْقُون» is a resumptive report; on casting the thing heard to the soothsayers, resumption is possible, and a ḥāl from «الشياطين» is possible, i.e. 'they descend upon every sinful liar, casting what they heard'." End. In his restricting resumption to the first meaning and allowing both possibilities for the second there is something to consider, because the permissibility of both possibilities applies to both meanings, so proof is needed for that.

semin-durr:224-224.t:
His saying: {يَتَّبِعُهُمُ}: It has already been covered that Nāfiʿ reads it with a light tāʾ, quiescent, and fatḥa on the bāʾ, in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf at His saying {لاَ يَتَّبِعُوكم} [al-Aʿrāf: 193], with the difference between the light and the heavy; let it be consulted there. Al-Ḥasan put sukūn on the ʿayn, and this is also reported from Abū ʿAmr, and it is not far from him, like {يَنْصُرْكم} [Āl ʿImrān: 160] and its kind. Hārūn reported from some of them fatḥa on the ʿayn, and it is a mistake. And the claim that the fatḥa is for assimilation of vowels (ittibāʿ) is an error.
The majority read «الشعُراءُ» in the nominative as a mubtadaʾ, the clause after it being the khabar. ʿĪsā read it in the accusative by way of ishtighāl (an occupying pronoun).

semin-durr:225-225.t:
His saying: {يَهِيمُونَ}: This clause may be the khabar of «أنَّ», and this is the apparent sense, because it is the focus of the benefit. «في كل وادٍ» is attached to it. It is also possible that «في كل وادٍ» is the khabar, with «يهيمون» a ḥāl from the pronoun in the khabar; the governor is what this khabar is attached to, or the preposition itself, as has been covered in its like more than once. It is also possible that the clause is a khabar after a khabar, according to those who allow multiple khabars without restriction. This belongs to the eloquent metaphor (istiʿāra) and splendid simile (tamthīl): he likened their roaming through the varieties of speech, the ways of praise, blame, simile and kinds of poetry, to the wandering of the one who wanders (hāʾim) in every valley and path.
Al-hāʾim is the one who goes astray in his travelling and does not aim at a specific place. «هام على وجهه» means he went away. The lover (ʿāshiq) is also called hāʾim, from this. Al-hayamān is the thirsty. Al-huyām is a disease that takes camels from thirst. One says «جمل أَهْيَمُ» and «ناقةٌ هَيْماءُ», and the plural of both is hīm. The Exalted said: {فَشَارِبُونَ شُرْبَ الهيم} [al-Wāqiʿa: 55]. And al-hayām of sand is the dry, as if they imagined in it the meaning of thirst.

semin-durr:227-227.t:
His saying: {أَيَّ مُنقَلَبٍ}: It is accusative as a maṣdar, and what makes it accusative is «يَنْقَلِبُون». It was fronted because it contains the meaning of a question. It is suspended (muʿalliq) from «سَيَعْلَمُ», standing in the place of its two objects. Abū l-Baqāʾ said: "«أيَّ مُنْقَلبٍ» is an adjective of an omitted maṣdar, i.e. 'they will turn about with a turning of what kind of turning'. And «سَيَعْلم» does not govern it, because what precedes an interrogative does not govern it." What he said is rejected: the ayy that occurs as an adjective is not interrogative, and likewise the interrogative is not an adjective of anything; rather they are two categories, each a category in itself. And «أيّ» is divided into many categories: the conditional; the interrogative; the relative; the adjectival and the described one according to al-Akhfash specifically; the vocative, as in «يا أيُّهذا»; and the one that links to the vocative a noun having al-, as in «يا أيُّها الرجلُ», according to everyone other than al-Akhfash. Al-Akhfash makes it relative in the vocative. I have treated that thoroughly in my commentary on al-Tashīl.
Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan read «أي مُنْفَلَتٍ يَنْفَلِتُون» with fāʾ and with tāʾ, from infilāt (escaping), and its meaning is clear. And Allah knows best.

semin-durr:1-1.t:
His saying: {طسم}: Ḥamza pronounced the nūn of {سِين} clearly before the mīm, as though intending a pause; otherwise assimilation of its like is obligatory. The rest assimilate it. The i'rab of the disconnected letters has already been given. In the codex of ʿAbd Allāh it is ṭ. s. m., each letter separate from the others. It was said: this is the reading of Abū Jaʿfar, meaning that he pauses on every letter with a pause that distinguishes each letter; otherwise it could not be imagined that it would be pronounced in the form it has in this orthography. ʿĪsā read, and it is related from Nāfiʿ, with kasra on the mīm, here and in al-Qaṣaṣ, as an indeclinable form. The two brothers (Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī) and Abū Bakr used imāla on the ṭāʾ. This has already been given.

[Translator's note: the source has a slash mark ("/") after "pause" in the first sentence; it appears to be a printing artefact and is not translated.]

semin-durr:4-4.t:
His saying: {إِن نَّشَأْ نُنَزِّلْ}: the majority read the nūn of majesty in both. It is related from Abū ʿAmr with yāʾ in both, that is, "If Allah wills, He will send down." In principle {إِنْ} enters upon what is doubtful, or upon what is certain but whose time is unspecified; the verse is of the latter kind.

His saying: {فَظَلَّتْ}: it is conjoined to {نُنَزِّلْ}, so it is jussive in position. It may also be resumptive, not conjoined to the apodosis. The first is supported by the reading of Ṭalḥa, {فَتَظْلِلْ}, an imperfect with the doubling undone.

His saying: {خَاضِعِينَ}: there are two views on it. One: that it is a khabar of {أَعْنَاقُهُمْ}. Its being in the sound plural was found problematic because that is restricted to rational beings. It was answered in several ways. First: that by "necks" is meant the chiefs, as it is said: "they have faces and chests." He said:

3505 - . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... في مَجْمَعٍ مِنْ نواصِي الخيلِ مَشْهودِ (… in an attended gathering of the forelocks of the horses)

Second: that there is an omitted muḍāf, that is, "so the owners of the necks remained", then it was omitted and the khabar stayed as it was before the omission of the one reported about, out of regard for the omitted. This was given shortly before in the reading {وَقُمْراً مُّنِيراً} [al-Furqān: 61]. Third: that when it was annexed to rational beings, it acquired this ruling from them, as the feminine is acquired by annexation to a feminine in his saying:

3506 - . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... كما شَرِقَتْ صَدْرُ القناةِ من الدمِ (… as the chest of the spear became stained with blood)

Fourth: that al-aʿnāq is the plural of ʿunuq of the people, meaning the group, so the limb is not meant at all. From it is his saying:

3507 - أنَّ العراقَ وأهلَه ... عُنُقٌ إليك فَهَيْتَ هَيْتا (That Iraq and its people are a ʿunuq (group) toward you, so come, come!)

I said: This is close to the meaning of the first, except that this speaker applies al-aʿnāq to a group of people absolutely, chiefs or others. Fifth: al-Zamakhsharī said: "The original of the speech is: 'so they remained submissive to it', and al-aʿnāq was inserted to show the place of submission, and the speech was left on its original form, like their saying 'the people of al-Yamāma went (dhahabat, feminine)', as though al-ahl were not mentioned." I said: There is something to be questioned in the comparison with "dhahabat ahlu l-Yamāma", because ahl is not at all inserted, since it is the thing intended by the ruling; as for the feminine, it is because it acquired the feminine. Sixth: that they were treated as rational beings when what is an act of rational beings was attributed to them, as in {سَاجِدِينَ} and {طَائِعِينَ} in Yūsuf and al-Sajda.

The second view: that it is accusative as a ḥāl from the pronoun in {أَعْنَاقُهُمْ}; so said al-Kisāʾī. Abū l-Baqāʾ considered it weak, saying: "Because {خَاضِعِينَ} would be running on other than the agent of {ظَلَّتْ}, so it needs the overt pronoun of the agent to be shown, and it would have been necessary to say 'khāḍiʿīna hum'." I said: {خَاضِعِينَ} runs, in expression and meaning, only upon the one to whom it belongs, namely the pronoun in {أَعْنَاقُهُمْ}; and the issue he raised is that the adjective runs on other than the one to whom it belongs in expression but not in meaning. So how does what he imposes follow? Even were it so, what he said would not follow, because al-Kisāʾī and the Kufans do not require the overt pronoun in this issue if confusion is avoided, so he would hold to what he was charged with; and had he considered it weak because a ḥāl comes from the muḍāf ilayhi, it would have been nearer. Yet it is not weak, because the muḍāf is a part of the muḍāf ilayhi, as in {مَا فِي صُدُورِهِم مِّنْ غِلٍّ إِخْوَاناً} [al-Ḥijr: 47].

semin-durr:5-5.t: His saying: {إِلاَّ كَانُواْ}: a circumstantial clause (jumla ḥāliyya). The investigation of this and of what is before it was given at the beginning of al-Anbiyāʾ.

semin-durr:7-7.t:
His saying: {كَمْ أَنبَتْنَا}: kam is for plurality, so it is khabariyya (declarative), and is accusative by what follows it as a direct object, that is, "many kinds We caused to grow." {مِن كُلِّ زَوْجٍ} is tamyīz (specification). Abū l-Baqāʾ allowed that it be a ḥāl, but that has no meaning.

al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you say: what is the meaning of combining kam and kull? Were it said 'We caused to grow in it of every kind'? I say: kull indicates the comprehension of the pairs of plants in detail, and kam indicates that this comprehended whole is abundant to excess."

semin-durr:10-10.t:
His saying: {وَإِذْ نادى}: the operative in it is implied. al-Zajjāj took it to be "Recite!" (utlu), and others "Remember!"

His saying: {أَنِ ائت}: it may be explicative (mufassira), and it may be maṣdariyya, that is, "by [saying] 'Go'".

semin-durr:11-11.t:
His saying: {قَوْمَ فِرْعَوْنَ}: a badal or ʿaṭf bayān of {القوم الظالمين}. Abū l-Baqāʾ said: "It is the object of {تَتَّقُونَ} on the reading of the one who read {تَتَّقُونَ} in the second person with fatḥa on the nūn, as will come. On this reading it may be a vocative."

His saying: {أَلا يَتَّقُونَ}: the majority read yāʾ in {يَتَّقُونَ} and fatḥa on the nūn, and what is meant is the people of Pharaoh. The object is omitted, that is, "they fear the punishment of …". ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muslim ibn Yasār, Ḥammād and Shaqīq ibn Salama read it with tāʾ from above (second person) by way of iltifāt, addressing them with it as a rebuke, the implied form being: "O people of Pharaoh!" Some read yattaqūni with yāʾ from below and kasra on the nūn. It has two explanations. One: that yattaqūni is an imperfect and its object is the yāʾ of the first-person speaker, with the kasra sufficing in its place. The second, which al-Zamakhsharī allowed: that yā is the vocative particle and ittaqūni is an imperative, as in "alā yā usjudū", that is, "O people, fear Me!" or "O men, fear Me!" The like of this will be investigated in al-Naml. This is a remote explanation.

This clause has two views. One: that it is resumptive, with no grammatical position. al-Zamakhsharī allowed it to be a ḥāl from the pronoun in {الظَّالِمِينَ}, that is, "they do wrong, not fearing Allah and His punishment", the hamza of denial (inkār) having entered upon the ḥāl. The Shaykh declared him mistaken on two counts. One: that it entails separation between the ḥāl and its operative by a foreign element of theirs, for he parsed {قَوْمَ فِرْعَوْنَ} as ʿaṭf bayān of {الْقَوْمَ الظَّالِمِينَ}. Two: that even granting that, it is not permissible, because what follows the hamza is not governed by what precedes it. He said: "Your saying 'I came, are you hastening?' — if you make 'hastening' governed by 'I came', it is not permissible; but if you imply an operative, it is permissible."

The apparent sense is that {أَلَا} is for offering (ʿarḍ). al-Zamakhsharī said: "It is the negative lā upon which the hamza of denial has entered." And it was said: it is for alerting (tanbīh).

[Translator's note: the source has a slash mark ("/") after "O people of Pharaoh"; it appears to be a printing artefact and is not translated.]

semin-durr:12-12.t: His saying: {أَن يُكَذِّبُونِ}: the object of {أَخَافُ}, that is, "I fear their calling me a liar."

semin-durr:13-13.t:
His saying: {وَيَضِيقُ صَدْرِي وَلاَ يَنطَلِقُ}: the majority read them nominative. There are two views. One: that it is resumptive, reporting that. The second: that it is conjoined to the khabar of {إِنَّ}. Zayd ibn ʿAlī, Ṭalḥa, ʿĪsā and al-Aʿmash read both accusative. al-Aʿraj read the first accusative and the second nominative. The accusative is a conjunction on the ṣila of {أَنْ}, so the three verbs, yukadhdhibūni, yaḍīqu and lā yanṭaliqu, all fall within the sphere of fear. al-Zamakhsharī said: "The difference between the two, that is, nominative and accusative, is that the nominative indicates that there are three reasons in it: the fear of being called a liar, the tightness of the chest, and the inability of the tongue to flow freely. The accusative implies that his fear is connected to these three. If you say: in the accusative the fear is connected to the three matters, and among them is the negation of the tongue's flowing, and the reality of fear is only a distress that reaches a person for a matter that will happen, and that was already happening, so how was it allowed to connect fear to it? I say: he connected the fear to their calling him a liar and to what would come to him because of it of tightness of the chest, and the impediment in the tongue is an addition to what he already had. In any case that impediment which was in him went away through his supplication. It was also said: a slight remnant of it remained. If you say: this excuse of yours is refuted by the nominative, because the meaning is 'I am afraid, tight of chest, my tongue not flowing'? I say: it is possible that this was before the supplication and its being answered; it is also possible that he intends the small amount that remained."

His saying: {فَأَرْسِلْ}: that is, "so send Jibrīl" or the angel, the direct object having been omitted.

semin-durr:15-15.t: His saying: {فاذهبا}: conjoined to what the particle of rebuke (ḥarf al-radʿ) indicates of the verb, as though it were said: "Be deterred from thinking (that), and go, you and your brother."

semin-durr:16-16.t:
His saying: {إِنَّا رَسُولُ}: he made {رَسُولُ} singular for several reasons: either because it is a maṣdar in the sense of risāla, and a maṣdar is singular. An instance of rasūl in the sense of risāla is his saying:

3508 - لقد كَذَبَ الواشُون ما فُهْتُ عندهمْ ... بِسِرٍّ ولا أَرْسَلْتُهُمْ برسولِ (The slanderers lied: I never spoke a secret in their presence, nor sent them with a message)

that is, with a message (risāla). Or because the two share one law, so they were treated as one messenger. Or because the meaning is that each one of us is a messenger. Or because it is a case of putting the singular in the place of the dual, because of their inseparability, so they became like two inseparable things such as the two eyes and the two hands. And where these meanings were not intended, he agreed in number, in His saying: {إِنَّا رَسُولاَ رَبِّكَ} [Ṭā Hā: 47].

semin-durr:17-17.t: His saying: {أَنْ أَرْسِلْ}: it may be explicative (mufassira) of {رَسُولُ}, if it is said to be in the sense of risāla (message): the two of them explained the message by this and clarified it by it. It may be maṣdariyya, that is, "a messenger with such-and-such."

semin-durr:18-18.t:
His saying: {وَلِيداً}: a ḥāl from the object of {نُرَبِّكَ}; it is a faʿīl in the sense of mafʿūl. al-Walīd: the boy, so named by what he was at the time.

His saying: {مِنْ عُمُرِكَ}: a ḥāl from {سِنِينَ}. Abū ʿAmr, in one transmission, read it with sukūn on the mīm for lightness from fuʿul.

semin-durr:19-19.t: al-Shaʿbī read {فِعْلَتَكَ} with kasra, on the pattern of manner (hayʾa), because it is a kind of killing, namely the blow (al-wakza). {وَأَنتَ مِنَ الكافرين} may be a ḥāl, and may be resumptive.

semin-durr:20-20.t:
His saying: {إِذاً وَأَنَاْ مِنَ الضالين}: idhan here is only a particle of response (ḥarf jawāb). al-Zamakhsharī said: "It is both response and requital (jazāʾ)." He said: "If you say: idhan is a particle of response and requital together, and the speech occurred as a reply to Pharaoh, so how did it come as requital? I say: Pharaoh's saying 'and you did your deed' contains the sense that you repaid my favour with what you did. So Mūsā said to him: 'Yes, I did it as one repaying you', conceding his statement, as though his favour were, in his view, worthy of being repaid with that sort of repayment."

The Shaykh said: "This is the position of Sībawayh, meaning that it is for requital and response together. He said: but the commentators on the Book understood that it may be without requital, while response is a meaning that is inseparable from it."

[Translator's note: the source has a slash mark ("/") after "repaid"; it appears to be a printing artefact and is not translated.]

semin-durr:21-21.t: His saying: {لَمَّا خِفْتُكُمْ}: the majority read it with doubled mīm; this is the lammā that is a particle of occurrence (ḥarf wujūb) according to Sībawayh, or in the sense of "when" (ḥīna) according to al-Fārisī. It is related from Ḥamza with kasra on the lām and a lightened mīm, that is, "because of my fear of you", with mā being maṣdariyya. This reading resembles his reading in Āl ʿImrān: {لِمَا آتَيْتُكُمْ}, which has already been given in full. ʿĪsā read {حُكُماً} with ḍamma on the kāf, by assimilation of the vowel (ittibāʿ).

semin-durr:22-22.t:
His saying: {وَتِلْكَ نِعْمَةٌ}: there are two views on it. One: that it is a statement by way of mockery, that is, "if there is any favour there, it is only that you made my people slaves to you." It was also said: the interrogative particle is omitted because the meaning is understood, that is, "Is that …?" This is the position of al-Akhfash, who counted among such cases the poet's saying:

3509 - أفرحُ أَنْ أُرْزَأَ الكرامَ . . . (Am I to rejoice that I lose the noble …)

This has been given at length in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ at His saying the Exalted {وَمَآ أَصَابَكَ مِن سَيِّئَةٍ فَمِن نَّفْسِكَ} [verse 79] and elsewhere.

His saying: {أَنْ عَبَّدتَّ}: there are several views on it. First: that it is nominative in position as ʿaṭf bayān of {تِلْكَ}, like His saying {وَقَضَيْنَآ إِلَيْهِ ذَلِكَ الأمر أَنَّ دَابِرَ هَؤُلآءِ مَقْطُوعٌ} [al-Ḥijr: 66]. Second: that it is accusative in position as mafʿūl li-ajlihi (object of purpose). Third: that it is a badal of {نِعْمَةٌ}. Fourth: that it is a badal of the hā in {تَمُنُّهَا}. Fifth: that it is genitive by an implied bāʾ, that is, "because you enslaved". Sixth: that it is the khabar of an implied mubtadaʾ, that is, "it is …". Seventh: that it is accusative by the implied "I mean" (aʿnī). The clause {تَمُنُّهَا} is an adjective of {نِعْمَةٌ}. {تَمُنُّ} governs with the bāʾ; it was said that it is omitted, i.e. tamunnu bihā; and it was said that tamunnu was made to include the meaning of "mention" (tadhkuru).

semin-durr:23-23.t: His saying: {وَمَا رَبُّ العالمين}: he used mā and not man only because mā is used to ask for the quiddity (māhiyya), as in your saying "What is the ʿanqāʾ?" And since the answer to this question could not be given in a possible way, Mūsā, peace be upon him, turned to an answer that was possible, so he answered with His attributes the Exalted, and singled out those attributes because no one shares them with Him the Exalted. In that is a refutation of Pharaoh's claim that he is a god. It was said: he did not understand the question, so he used mā and not man; this is nothing. It was said: he only asked about attributes; Abū l-Baqāʾ mentioned this. This too is nothing, because the rhetoricians stated that mā is used to ask about quiddities, and man did come in His saying {فَمَن رَّبُّكُمَا يَا مُوسَى} [Ṭā Hā: 49].

semin-durr:24-24.t:
His saying: {وَمَا بَيْنَهُمَآ}: the dual pronoun refers back to two plurals, regarding the two genera, as the poet did overtly in his saying:

3510 - . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... بين رِماحَيْ مالِكٍ ونَهْشَلِ (… between the spears of Mālik and Nahshal)

semin-durr:29-29.t: His saying: {لأَجْعَلَنَّكَ مِنَ المسجونين}: he turned away from la-asjunannaka ("I will imprison you"), which is more specific than it, only because it contains an emphasis that the other lacks; or its meaning is "I will make you one of those whose condition you know in my prisons."

semin-durr:30-30.t: His saying: {أَوَلَوْ جِئْتُكَ}: this is the wāw of ḥāl. al-Ḥūfī said: "It is for conjunction." The investigation of this has already been given at His saying {أَوَلَوْ كَانَ آبَاؤُهُمْ} [verse 170] in al-Baqara. Most of the clauses here have already been parsed.

semin-durr:34-34.t: His saying: {حَوْلَهُ}: a ḥāl from {الْمَلَإِ}. The object of the saying is His saying {إِنَّ هَذَا لَسَاحِرٌ عَلِيمٌ}. It was also said: it is a ṣila of {الْمَلَإِ}, since it is in the sense of "who/that" (alladhī). It was also said: the relative noun is omitted; these are two views of the Kufans.

semin-durr:44-44.t: His saying: {بِعِزَّةِ فِرْعَونَ}: it may be an oath, its answer being {إِنَّا لَنَحْنُ الْغَالِبُونَ}. It may also be attached to an omitted element, that is, "we shall prevail by means of his might", as indicated by what follows it. It is not permissible for it to be attached to {الْغَالِبُونَ}, because what is within the sphere of inna cannot be put before it.

semin-durr:46-46.t:
His saying: {فَأُلْقِيَ}: al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you say: who is the agent of the throwing, if it were stated explicitly? I say: it is Allah, Mighty and Majestic." Then he said: "And you may also not imply an agent, because {أُلْقُوا} means 'they fell down and dropped'." The Shaykh said: "This is nothing, because a verb is not built in the passive unless it has an agent for which the object stands in. As for saying that no agent is implied for it, that is a statement that has strayed from the right." 

His saying: {فَإِذَا هِيَ تَلْقَفُ}: their disagreement about it has already been given. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said here: "al-Bazzī and Ibn Fulayḥ, from Ibn Kathīr, read it with the tāʾ doubled, fatḥa on the lām and the qāf doubled. On this reading, when beginning, the hamzat al-waṣl must be dropped, yet the hamzat al-waṣl does not enter imperfect verbs, as it does not enter active participles." The Shaykh said: "It is as though he imagines that it is not possible to begin a word except by bringing the hamzat al-waṣl, and this is not necessary; often continuing (waṣl) differs from stopping (waqf), and stopping differs from continuing, and one who is practised in the readings knows that." I said: He means His saying {فَإِذَا هِيَ تَلْقَفُ}, for al-Bazzī doubles the tāʾ, since the original is tatalaqqafu with two tāʾs, and he assimilated; so if he stops at {هِيَ} and begins with tatalaqqafu, he should undo the assimilation and not assimilate, lest he begin with a sākin, which is not possible. Ibn ʿAṭiyya's statement, "On this reading it must …" to the end, is a weakening of the reading for what he mentioned, that the hamzat al-waṣl does not enter the imperfect verb and one cannot begin with a sākin, and so it was weakened. The Shaykh's answer, denying the necessity, is good, except that he should have replaced the word "stopping" with "beginning", because that is what the speech was about, I mean beginning with the word {تَّلَقَّفُ}.

[Translator's note: the source has a slash mark ("/") after "the readings"; it appears to be a printing artefact and is not translated.]

semin-durr:51-51.t:
His saying: {أَن كُنَّآ}: the majority read {أَنْ} with fatḥa, that is, "because we are the first in speaking of faith". Abān ibn Taghlib and Abū Muʿādh read it with kasra on the hamza. There are two views on it. One: that it is conditional, its apodosis omitted because the meaning is understood, or put first according to those who allow that. The second: that it is the lightened form of the heavy (inna), and the distinguishing lām (al-lām al-fāriqa) is dispensed with because the meaning guides toward affirmation rather than negation, as in:

3511 - . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... وإنْ مالِكٌ كانَتْ كرامَ المعادنِ (… and indeed Mālik's people were of noble stock)

and in the hadith: "إن كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يحب العسل" ("The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to love honey"), that is, la-yuḥibbuhu.

semin-durr:53-53.t: His saying: {حَاشِرِينَ}: it is the object of {أَرْسَلَ}, and {حَاشِرِينَ} means "gathering the magicians".

semin-durr:54-54.t:
His saying: {إِنَّ هؤلاء لَشِرْذِمَةٌ}: governed by an implied saying, that is, "he said: these are …". This saying may be a ḥāl, that is, "he sent them saying that", and may be explicative of {أَرْسَلَ}. al-Shirdhima: a group of people. It was said: any remnant of something paltry is called a shirdhima, and it is said "a shardhim garment", that is, tattered (akhlāq). He said:

3512 - جاء الشتاءُ وقميصي أُخْلاقْ ... شراذِمٌ يضحكُ منه الخَلاَّقْ (Winter came and my shirt was in tatters, shreds at which the fuller laughs)

And Abū ʿUbayda recited:

3513 - [يُحْذَيْنَ] في شَراذِمِ النِّعالِ ... (… [they are shod] in the shreds of sandals)

semin-durr:56-56.t:
His saying: {حَاذِرُونَ}: the Kufans and Ibn Dhakwān read ḥādhirūn with an alif, and the rest ḥadhirūn without it. Abū ʿUbayda said: "They have one meaning; one says rajulun ḥadhirun, ḥadhurun and ḥādhirun in the same sense." It was said: rather there is a difference between them: al-ḥadhir is the one who is alert, and al-ḥādhir is the one who is afraid. It was also said: al-ḥadhir is one created and moulded on caution, while al-ḥādhir is one to whom it happens incidentally. It was also said: al-ḥadhir is the one who is armed, that is, who has the might of weapons. Sībawayh recited, for the operation of ḥadhir as an intensive pattern transformed from ḥādhir, his saying:

3514 - حَذِرٌ أموراً لا تَضِيْرُ وآمِنٌ ... ما ليسَ مُنْجِيَه من الأَقْدارِ (Wary of matters that do not harm, and feeling safe from what will not save him from the decrees)

Some have claimed that when Sībawayh asked him whether he knew anything about the operation of faʿil, he composed this verse for him. Sībawayh was then reproached: how does he take fabricated evidence? This is a mistake, for this person confessed against himself to lying, so his statement does not impugn Sībawayh. The one who claimed to have composed the verse is al-Lāḥiqī. ḥadhira is transitive by itself; the Exalted said {يَحْذَرُ الآخِرَةَ} [al-Zumar: 9], and al-ʿAbbās ibn Mirdās said:

3515 - وإني حاذِرٌ أَنْمِيْ سِلاحي ... إلى أوصالِ ذَيَّالٍ مَنيعِ (I am wary, I raise my weapon to the limbs of a long-tailed, impregnable one)

Ibn al-Samayfaʿ and Ibn Abī ʿAmmār read ḥādirūn with the unpointed dāl, from their saying ʿaynun ḥadra, meaning "large", as in:

3516 - وعَيْنٌ لها حَدْرَةٌ بَدْرَةٌ ... (And an eye with a large, full (pupil) …)

and the meaning is "large". It was also said: al-ḥādir: the strong, the full. It is related: rajulun ḥādirun, that is, full of rage; and rajulun ḥādirun, that is, a fool, as though full of foolishness. He said:

3517 - أُحِبُّ الغلامَ السَّوْءَ من أجلِ أُمِّه ... وأُبْغِضُهُ من بُغْضِها وهو حادِرُ (I love the bad boy for his mother's sake, and I hate him from her hatred, though he is ḥādir)

It is also said: rajulun ḥadhur, on the pattern of yaqiẓ, an intensive of ḥādhir, with this meaning. I said: so it has come to be said ḥadhira, ḥadhura and ḥādhir, with the pointed and the unpointed dāl, and the meaning differs.

semin-durr:58-58.t: His saying: {وَمَقَامٍ}: the majority read it with fatḥa on the mīm, which is a place of standing; Qatāda and al-Aʿraj read it with ḍamma, which is a place of residence.

semin-durr:59-59.t:
His saying: {كَذَلِكَ}: there are three views on it. al-Zamakhsharī said: "It admits three views: the accusative, as 'We brought them out in the likeness of that bringing-out which We described'; the genitive, as an adjective of {مَقَامٍ}, that is, 'and a noble station like that station which they had'; and the nominative, as the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, that is, 'the matter is thus'." The Shaykh said: "The first view is not allowable, because it comes down to likening a thing to itself, and likewise the second view, because the station they had is the noble station, so a thing is not likened to itself." I said: There is no likening of a thing to itself in that, because what is meant in the first is 'We brought them out with a bringing-out like the well-known, famous bringing-out', and likewise the second.

[Translator's note: the source has a slash mark ("/") in the Shaykh's quotation after "because"; it appears to be a printing artefact and is not translated.]

His saying: {وَأَوْرَثْنَاهَا}: conjoined to {فَأَخْرَجْنَاهُمْ}.

semin-durr:60-60.t:
His saying: {فَأَتْبَعُوهُم}: the majority read it with hamzat al-qaṭʿ, from atbaʿahu, that is, "he made him follow himself", the second object being omitted. It was said: atbaʿahu is said in the sense of ittabaʿahu with hamzat al-waṣl, that is, "he caught up with him". al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥārith al-Dhimārī read it with hamzat al-waṣl and a doubled tāʾ, and it is in the sense of "catching up".

His saying: {مُّشْرِقِينَ}: accusative as a ḥāl. The apparent sense is that it is from the agent. The meaning of mushriqīn is "entering into the time of sunrise", like aṣbaḥa and amsā, that is, entered into these two times. It was said: "entering the east", like anjada and atʾhama. And it was said: mushriqīn in the sense of "shining". In the exegesis: the Children of Israel were in light and the Copts in darkness; on this, {مُّشْرِقِينَ} would be a ḥāl from the object. In my view it may be a ḥāl from both the agent and the object, if we make mushriqīn mean "entering into the time of sunrise" or "into the place of the east", because each of the two parties was entering that time or that place.

semin-durr:61-61.t:
His saying: {فَلَمَّا تَرَاءَى الجمعان}: the majority read {تَرَاءَى} with the hamza fully pronounced; Ibn Waththāb and al-Aʿmash read it without hamza. Its explanation is that the hamza is made light "between-between" (bayna bayna), not a pure replacement, so that three alifs do not come together: the first, the augment after the rāʾ; the second, replacing the hamza; and the third, the lām of the word; but the third does not stay in continuous reading, being omitted due to the meeting of two quiescents. Then the readers differed about the imāla of this letter, and I say: this letter is either stopped upon or not. If it is stopped upon, Ḥamza uses imāla on its last alif because it is a final one converted from yāʾ. It is necessary in its imāla that the fatḥa of the softened hamza be given imāla, because when one stops at the like of such a hamza he softens it according to his position, and he gives imāla to the first alif by following the imāla of the fatḥa of the hamza; and it is necessary in its imāla that the fatḥa of the rāʾ before it be given imāla. This is imāla for the sake of imāla.

The other readers do not use imāla on any of that, while the analogy of al-Kisāʾī's position is that he use imāla on the last alif and the fatḥa of the hamza before it. So Ibn al-Bādhish transmitted from him and from Ḥamza. If it is connected: its last alif goes because of the meeting of two quiescents, and with its going, the imāla of the fatḥa of the hamza goes, and the imāla of the augmented alif remains; and the imāla of the fatḥa of the rāʾ before it, in his view, is by taking the omitted alif into account. At that point it is said: the cause was dropped and the caused remained; since the imāla of the first alif was only because of the imāla of the last alif, as was established earlier, and the last has gone, so the first should not have imāla since what required it has gone; but he took the omitted into account and made it equal to the pronounced. That is why Abū Ḥātim assailed it and said: "Reading this letter with imāla is impossible." I said: Something resembling this procedure was given earlier in al-Anʿām at {رَأَى الْقَمَرَ} and {رَأَى الشَّمْسَ}; so look to it there.

His saying: {لَمُدْرَكُونَ}: the majority read it with sukūn on the dāl, a passive participle of adraka, that is, "overtaken". al-Aʿraj and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read it with fatḥa on the dāl, doubled, and kasra on the rāʾ. al-Zamakhsharī said: "The meaning: following one another in perishing at their hands. Of it is the verse from al-Ḥamāsa:

3518 - أَبَعْدَ بَني أمِّي الذين تتابَعُوا ... أُرَجِّيْ الحياةَ أم مِنْ الموتِ أجْزَعُ (After the sons of my mother, who followed one another (in death), do I hope for life, or do I fear death?)

meaning: iddaraka on the pattern ifta ʿala is intransitive in the sense of 'perished and vanished'. One says iddaraka l-shayʾu yaddarikuhu, so he is muddarik, that is, perished successively; and for this reason the rāʾ has kasra." Among those who stated expressly the kasra of it is Abū l-Faḍl al-Rāzī, who said: "iddaraka on ifta ʿala may also be in the sense of afʿala, transitive; had the reading been from this, the rāʾ would have had to be fatḥa. It has not reached me from the two of them, meaning al-Aʿraj and ʿUbayd, except kasra."

semin-durr:63-63.t:
His saying: {فانفلق}: before it is an omitted clause, that is, "so he struck, and it split." Ibn ʿUṣfūr claimed that what is omitted is only "struck" and the fāʾ of "split", and that the fāʾ present is the fāʾ of "so he struck"; so he kept from each that which indicates the omitted: he kept the fāʾ of "so he struck" to point to "struck", and he kept "split" to point to the fāʾ attached to it. This is a collapsing statement.

The readers differed on making the rāʾ of {فِرْقٍ} light (tarqīq), on the authority of Warsh, because of the qāf. It was also read filq with lām in place of the rāʾ, to agree with {فَانفَلَقَ}. al-Ṭawd: the great mountain, towering in the sky.

[Translator's note: the source has a slash mark ("/") after "great"; it appears to be a printing artefact and is not translated.]

semin-durr:64-64.t: His saying: {وَأَزْلَفْنَا}: that is, "We brought near to safety". {ثَمَّ} is an adverb of distant place. {الآخَرِينَ} are Mūsā and his companions. al-Ḥasan and Abū Ḥaywa read {وَزَلَفْنَا}, triliteral. Ubayy, Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥārith read it with qāf, that is, azlalnā ("We made slip"). By "the others" in this reading are meant Pharaoh and his people.

semin-durr:70-70.t:
His saying: {إِذْ قَالَ}: the operative in {إِذْ} is {نَبَأَ} or "Recite!" (utlu). So al-Ḥūfī said. This is possible only if {إِذْ} is a direct object. It was said: {إِذْ} is a badal of {نَبَأَ}, a badal of inclusion (badal ishtimāl). It amounts to its being governed by "Recite!" with the interpretation mentioned.

His saying: {وَقَوْمِهِ}: the hāʾ refers to Ibrāhīm, because he is the one being spoken about. It was said: it refers to his father, because he is the nearest mentioned, that is, "he said to his father and to his father's people." It is supported by {إِنِّي أَرَاكَ وَقَوْمَكَ} [al-Anʿām: 74], where he annexed the people to him.
