semin-durr:71-71.t: His saying: {نَعْبُدُ أَصْنَاماً}: they came in the answer with the verb stated explicitly so as to conjoin to it their saying {فَنَظَلُّ}, out of pride in it and delight in it; otherwise their saying "idols" would have been enough, like His saying the Exalted {قُلِ الْعَفْوَ} [al-Baqara: 219] and {قَالُوا خَيْراً} [al-Naḥl: 30].

semin-durr:72-72.t:
His saying: {هَلْ يَسْمَعُونَكُمْ}: there must be something omitted, that is, "do they hear your supplication", or "do they hear you supplicating?" On the first implied form, it governs one object by agreement; on the second, it governs two, with the implied clause standing in for the second. This is the position of al-Fārisī. According to others the implied clause is a ḥāl. The investigation of both views has already been given. Qatāda and Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmur read it with ḍamma on the yāʾ and kasra on the mīm, the second object omitted, that is, "do they make you hear the answer?"

His saying: {إِذْ تَدْعُونَ}: accusative by what precedes it; what is before it and what is after it are both past in meaning, though future in expression, by the operation of the first on {إِذْ}, and the operation of {إِذْ} on the second. Some said: {إِذْ} here is in the sense of idhā. al-Zamakhsharī said: "It is on the narration of a past state, and its meaning is: 'Bring to mind the [past] states in which you used to call on them, and say: did they hear you, or make you hear?' It is more effective in reproach." It has already been given that it was read with assimilation of the dhāl of idh and with its being clear before the tāʾ. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "The analogy of muddakir and the like is possible in it, but no one has read it so. The analogy would be for the pronunciation to be 'iddadʿūna'; what prevented this pronunciation is the connection of the radical dāl in the verb, so the similar letters became many." I said: he means that the pronunciation would then have a doubled unpointed dāl and then a quiescent unpointed dāl.

The Shaykh said: "This is not allowable, because this replacement is only in the tāʾ of ifta ʿala after dāl, dhāl and zāy, such as iddahana, iddakara and izdajara, and after jīm irregularly, such as 'ijdamaʿū' for 'ijtamaʿū'; or in the tāʾ of the pronoun after dāl and zāy, such as 'fuzdu' for 'fuztu' and 'jaladdu' for 'jaladtu'; or the tāʾ of 'tawlaj', of which they said 'dawlaj'. The tāʾ of the imperfect is none of what he mentioned. His statement 'what prevented … ' to the end implies that it is permissible if what he mentioned were not found; and on the implication of his statement you could say, for 'idh takhruj', 'iddakhruj', and no one says that; rather they say 'ittakhruj', assimilating the dhāl into the tāʾ."

semin-durr:74-74.t: His saying: {كَذَلِكَ}: accusative by {يَفْعَلُونَ}, that is, "they do the like of what we do." {يَفْعَلُونَ} is accusative in position as the second object of {وَجَدْنَا}.

semin-durr:77-77.t:
His saying: {عَدُوٌّ}: the higher dialect is to use ʿaduww in the singular and masculine. The Exalted said: {هُمُ الْعَدُوُّ} [al-Munāfiqūn: 4]. That was done with it only by likening it to verbal nouns such as al-walūʿ and al-qabūl. It may also be said aʿdāʾ and ʿaduwwa. His saying {عَدُوٌّ لِي} is on its original form, with no implied muḍāf and no inversion. It was said: idols do not show enmity, being inanimate, so the implied form is "their worshippers are an enemy to me." And it was said: rather there is an inversion in the speech, its implied form being "I am an enemy to them." These two are the weaker, because the speech is sound without them.

His saying: {إِلاَّ رَبَّ العالمين}: there are two views on it. One: that it is disconnected (munqaṭiʿ), that is, "but the Lord of the Worlds is not an enemy to me." al-Jurjānī said: "There is fronting and delaying in it, that is: 'Do you see what you worshipped, you and your ancient forefathers — except the Lord of the Worlds — for they are an enemy to me', with illā meaning 'other than' (dūna) and 'besides' (siwā)." The second: that it is connected. This is the position of al-Zajjāj, because they used to worship Allah the Exalted and the idols.

[Translator's note: the source has a slash mark ("/") after "meaning" in al-Jurjānī's statement; it appears to be a printing artefact and is not translated.]

semin-durr:78-78.t:
His saying: {الذي خَلَقَنِي}: there are several views on it: accusative as an adjective of {رَبَّ الْعَالَمِينَ}, or a badal, or ʿaṭf bayān, or by the implied "I mean"; and nominative as the khabar of an implied mubtadaʾ, that is, "He is the One who created me", or as a mubtadaʾ.

His saying: {فَهُوَ يَهْدِينِ}: a nominal clause, nominative in position as its khabar. al-Ḥūfī said: "The fāʾ entered because of what the mubtadaʾ includes of the sense of the condition." This is rejected, because the relative is specific, not general, and because the ṣila cannot have renewal in it, so it does not resemble the condition. Abū l-Baqāʾ followed al-Ḥūfī but did not address the fāʾ. If he meant what al-Ḥūfī meant, then what is in it has been given; and if he did not mean it, he follows al-Akhfash in allowing the redundant fāʾ in the khabar absolutely, such as "Zaydun fa-ḍribhu", and its investigation has already been given.

semin-durr:79-79.t:
His saying: {وَالَّذِي هُوَ يُطْعِمُنِي}: it may be a mubtadaʾ with its khabar omitted, and likewise what follows it. It may be that these are attributes of {الَّذِي خَلَقَنِي}. The entry of the wāw is permissible; its investigation has been given at the beginning of al-Baqara, as in:

3519 - إلى المَلِكِ القَرْمِ وابنِ الهُمامِ ... وليثِ الكتيبةِ في المُزْدَحَمْ (To the king, the chief, and son of the noble one, and lion of the battalion in the throng)

Ibn Abī Isḥāq retained the yāʾ of the first-person speaker in {يَسْقِينِ}, {يَشْفِينِ} and {يُحْيِينِ}, and this is also related from ʿĀṣim. The majority read {خَطِيئَتِي} in the singular. al-Ḥasan read khaṭāyāya, a broken plural.

semin-durr:85-85.t: His saying: {مِن وَرَثَةِ}: it is either a second object, that is, "settled" or "being among the heirs", or an adjective of an omitted element which is the second object, that is, "an heir from among the heirs".

semin-durr:88-88.t: His saying: {يَوْمَ لاَ يَنفَعُ}: a badal of {يَوْمَ} before it. Ibn ʿAṭiyya made this part of the speech of Allah the Exalted up to the end of the verses, while parsing {يَوْمَ لَا يَنفَعُ} as a badal of {يَوْمِ يُبْعَثُونَ}. The Shaykh rejected it, because the operative in the badal is the operative in the one substituted for, or another like it implied; and on both views it is not sound, because of the difference of speakers.

semin-durr:89-89.t:
His saying: {إِلاَّ مَنْ أَتَى الله}: there are several views on it. First: that it is disconnected (munqaṭiʿ), that is, "but whoever comes to Allah with a sound heart, that will benefit him." al-Zamakhsharī said: "In addition to that you must imply a muḍāf, namely the state, by which soundness is meant, and it is not of the genus of wealth and children, so that the meaning would come to: wealth and children do not benefit, only soundness of heart benefits; and had the muḍāf not been implied, the exception would not have gained a meaning."

The Shaykh said: "There is no necessity calling for omitting the muḍāf as he mentioned." I said: He implied the muḍāf only so that it would be imagined that the excepted is included in that from which the exception is made, for unless that is imagined, the exception does not occur; that is why they forbade "the horses neighed except the camels" unless by interpretation.

Second: that it is a direct object of {لَا يَنفَعُ}, that is, "wealth and children do not benefit except this person, for it benefits him: his wealth spent in the ways of righteousness, and his righteous sons, because he taught them and was good to them." Third: that it is a badal from the omitted object, or from that from which the exception is made, since the implied form is: "neither wealth nor children benefit anyone of the people except one with this description." The one excepted from is omitted, as in his saying:

3520 - . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... ولم يَنْجُ إلاَّ جَفْنَ سيفٍ ومِئْزرا (… and he escaped with nothing but a sword sheath and a waist-wrapper)

that is, "he did not escape with anything". Fourth: that it is a badal of the agent of {يَنفَعُ}, so it is nominative. Abū l-Baqāʾ said: "He gave precedence to the rational, so the implied form is: 'except the wealth of whoever', or 'the sons of whoever', for he benefits himself and others by intercession."

I said: Abū l-Baqāʾ mixed one view with another: when we wish to make it a badal of the agent of {يَنفَعُ}, we have two ways. One: the way of precedence (taghlīb), i.e. we give the sons precedence over the wealth, and the exception is made from the sons, as though it were said: "the sons do not benefit except the son who comes with a sound heart, for he benefits himself by his righteousness and others by intercession." The second way: that you imply an omitted muḍāf before {مَنْ}, that is, "except the wealth of whoever" or "the sons of whoever"; so the views become five.

al-Zamakhsharī justified the connected sense of the exception in two ways. One: "except the state of whoever comes to Allah with a sound heart," and this is from his saying:

3521 - . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... تَحِيَّةُ بَيْنِهِمْ ضَرْبٌ وَجِيعُ (… their greeting to one another is a painful blow)

"and its reward is only the sword", and an example is that it be said: "Does Zayd have wealth and children?" and it is answered: "His wealth and sons are the soundness of his heart." You mean the negation of wealth and children from him and the affirmation of soundness of his heart in place of that. The second: he said: "If you wish, you may carry the speech by meaning and make wealth and children in the sense of riches, as though it were said: 'on a day when no wealth benefits except the wealth of the one who comes', because a man's wealth in his religion is the soundness of his heart, as his wealth in his worldly life is his money and his sons."

semin-durr:91-91.t: His saying: {وَبُرِّزَتِ}: Mālik ibn Dīnār read {وَبَرَزَتْ} with fatḥa on the bāʾ and a light rāʾ, active, ascribed to {الْجَحِيمُ}, which is why it is nominative.

semin-durr:94-94.t:
His saying: {فَكُبْكِبُواْ}: that is, they were thrown and overturned one upon another. al-Zamakhsharī said: "al-Kabkaba is the repetition of al-kabb. He made the repetition in the expression an indication of repetition in the meaning." Ibn ʿAṭiyya said something similar, saying: "This is the correct view, because the repetition of the verb is evident, as in ṣarra and ṣarṣara." This is the position of al-Zajjāj. In the like of this pattern there are three positions. One: this one. The second, the position of the Basrans: that all the letters are radical. The third, the position of the Kufans: that the third is a replacement for a letter like the second, so the original of kabkaba is kabbaba with three bāʾs; similarly lamlama and kafkafa. This is when the meaning remains sound with the dropping of the third; but if the meaning is not sound with its dropping, all are radical without disagreement, such as simsim and khimkhim.

The wāw of {كُبْكِبُوا}: it was said to refer to the idols, treating them as rational beings; and it was said: to their worshippers.

[Translator's note: the source has a slash mark ("/") after "one"; it appears to be a printing artefact and is not translated.]

semin-durr:96-96.t: His saying: {وَهُمْ فِيهَا يَخْتَصِمُونَ}: a circumstantial clause (jumla ḥāliyya) parenthetical between the saying and what it governs; what it governs is the oath clause.

semin-durr:97-97.t: His saying: {إِن كُنَّا لَفِي}: the position of the Basrans is that {إِنْ} is the lightened form and the lām is the distinguishing lām; the position of the Kufans is that {إِنْ} is negative and the lām is in the sense of illā.

semin-durr:98-98.t: His saying: {إِذْ نُسَوِّيكُمْ}: {إِذْ} is accusative, either by {مُبِينٍ} or by an omitted element, that is, "we were astray at the time of our equating you with Allah in worship." It may, though weakly, be governed by {ضَلَالٍ}, and the meaning is according to it. But its weakness is a technical one: that a described maṣdar does not operate after its description.

semin-durr:101-101.t:
His saying: {حَمِيمٍ}: al-ḥamīm is the near, from their saying "ḥāmmatu fulān", that is, his intimates. al-Zamakhsharī said: "al-Ḥamīm is from ihtimām (concern), and it is from the concern; or from al-ḥāmma, which is the intimate circle; and it is the sincere friend." The negation here may be a negation of the friend altogether, or of his attribute only, so it belongs to the chapter of:

3522 - على لاحِبٍ لا يهتدى بمنارِه ... (On a clear road not guided by its signposts …)

al-Ṣadīq may be singular, and may be used for the plural, as ʿaduww is used for it; one says hum ṣadīq and hum ʿaduww.

semin-durr:102-102.t:
His saying: {فَلَوْ أَنَّ}: it may be the one imbued with the meaning of wishing (tamannī), in which case it has no apodosis according to the well-known view, and the accusative of {فَنَكُونَ} is the answer to the wish which {لَوْ} conveys. It may be on its regular footing, its apodosis omitted, that is, "we would have found intercessors and friends" or "we would have done righteousness." On this the accusative of the verb is by an implied {أَنْ} conjoined to {كَرَّةً}, that is, "if we had a return, and so we would be", like her saying:

3523 - لَلُبْسُ عَباءةٍ وتَقَرَّ عيني ... (Wearing a cloak, and my eye being cooled …)

semin-durr:105-105.t: His saying: {كَذَّبَتْ قَوْمُ}: he made the verb of qawm feminine only because it is feminine, by the evidence of its diminutive quwayma. It was said: because it is in the sense of "community" (umma). And since its individual members are rational, male and female, the pronoun returns to it by giving precedence to the masculine, so it was said {لَهُمْ أَخُوهُمْ}. The object of {تَتَّقُونَ} is omitted, that is, "do you not fear Allah's punishment?"

semin-durr:111-111.t:
His saying: {وَاتَّبَعَكَ الأَرْذَلُونَ}: a circumstantial clause, from the kāf of {لَكَ}. ʿAbd Allāh, Ibn ʿAbbās and Abū Ḥaywa read {وَأَتْبَاعُكَ} nominative, the plural of tābiʿ like ṣāḥib and aṣḥāb, or of tabīʿ like sharīf and ashrāf, or of tabaʿ like baram and abrām. In its being nominative there are two views. One: that it is a mubtadaʾ and {الأَرْذَلُونَ} its khabar; the clause is also circumstantial. The second: that it is conjoined to the nominative pronoun in {نُؤْمِنُ}, and the separation by the preposition made that good; and {الأَرْذَلُونَ} is its adjective.

The Yemeni read {وَأَتْبَاعِكَ} genitive, conjoined to the kāf in {لَكَ}. That is weak, or forbidden according to the Basrans. On this, {الأَرْذَلُونَ} is nominative as the khabar of an implied mubtadaʾ, that is, "they are the lowliest." The root of al-arthal has already been given in Hūd.

semin-durr:112-112.t: His saying: {وَمَا عِلْمِي}: {مَا} admits two views. One, which is the apparent sense: that it is interrogative, nominative in position as a mubtadaʾ, with {عِلْمِي} its khabar, and the bāʾ attached to it. The second: that it is negative, with the bāʾ also attached to {عِلْمِي}. So al-Ḥūfī said, and it needs an implied khabar so that the speech becomes a clause with it.

semin-durr:113-113.t:
His saying: {لَوْ تَشْعُرُونَ}: its apodosis is omitted, and the object of {تَشْعُرُونَ} too.

al-Aʿraj and Abū Zurʿa read {لَوْ يَشْعُرُونَ} with the yāʾ of the third person, which is an iltifāt (shift of person). It is not good for it to refer back to the believers.

semin-durr:118-118.t:
His saying: {فَتْحاً}: it may be a direct object, in the sense of "that which is opened", and may be a confirmatory maṣdar.

His saying: {وَنَجِّنِي}: that from which one is saved is omitted because the meaning is understood, that is, "from what will befall my people." {مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ} is a clarification (bayān) of His saying {مَنْ مَعِي}.

[Translator's note: the source has a slash mark ("/") after "opened"; it appears to be a printing artefact and is not translated.]

semin-durr:119-119.t: His saying: {الْمَشْحُونِ}: that is, filled, loaded. One says: shaḥanahā ʿalayhim khaylan wa-rijālan ("he filled it against them with horses and men"). al-Shaḥnāʾ: enmity, because it fills the chests with rancour. al-Fulk here is singular, by the evidence of its being described with a singular; the discussion of it has already been given in al-Baqara.

semin-durr:128-128.t:
His saying: {تَعْبَثُونَ}: a circumstantial clause from the agent of {تَبْنُونَ}. al-Rīʿ, with kasra or fatḥa on the rāʾ, is the plural of rīʿa. In the language it is the elevated place. Dhū l-Rumma said:

3524 - طِراقُ الخَوافي مُشْرِفٌ فوقَ رِيْعَةٍ ... ندى ليلِه في رِيْشه يَتَرَقْرَقُ (Layer upon layer of feathers beneath, looking out over a high place, the dew of its night glistening on its feathers)

Abū ʿUbayda said: "It is the road," and recited for al-Musayyab ibn ʿAlas, describing women's litters:

3525 - في الآلِ يَخْفِضُها ويَرْفَعُهما ... رِيْعٌ يَلُوْحُ كأنه سَحْلُ (In the mirage, a rīʿ lowers them and raises them, gleaming as though it were a saḥl)

The commentators differed in expressing it, with many views. al-Rayʿ, with fatḥa: what accrues of tribute (kharāj).
